'''Thomas Arthur McMahon''' (April 21, 1943 – February 14, 1999) was an author and the Gordon McKay Professor of [[Applied Mechanics]] and Professor of Biology at [[Harvard University]]. He was born in [[Dayton, Ohio]], and grew up in [[Lexington, Massachusetts]].<ref name="Howe">{{cite journal |last1=Howe |first1=Robert D. |last2=Kronauer |first2=Richard E. |title=Thomas McMahon: A Dedication in Memoriam |journal=Annual Review of Biomedical Engineering |date=August 2001 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=xv–xxxix |doi=10.1146/annurev.bioeng.3.1.0 |s2cid=19491005 |url=http://www.annualreviews.org/doi/full/10.1146/annurev.bioeng.3.1.0 |access-date=21 February 2023 |language=en |issn=1523-9829|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A pioneer in biomechanics, McMahon studied [[terrestrial locomotion]] and the [[allometry|relationship of body size to shape]] and helped to develop devices for cardiac assistance and orthopedic biomechanics. He used simple mathematical models to explain complex phenomena and validated his models through experiments.<ref name="Howe"/> 
His book ''[[Muscles, Reflexes and Locomotion]]'' is considered a classic on the mathematics, chemistry, biology, and mechanics of [[animal locomotion]].<ref name="Thomas"/>
His work with [[basilisk lizards]] showed how they run on water.<ref name="Spinney">{{cite news |last1=Spinney |first1=Laura |title=Science: How speedy lizards take flight across water |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg14920232-800-science-how-speedy-lizards-take-flight-across-water/ |access-date=21 February 2023 |work=New Scientist |date=30 March 1996}}</ref><ref name="Crimson">{{cite news |title=Prof. McMahon, 'Tuned Track' Creator, Dies at 55 &#124; News &#124; The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1999/2/19/prof-mcmahon-tuned-track-creator-dies/ |access-date=21 February 2023 |work=The Harvard Crimson |date=February 19, 1999}}</ref>

McMahon was the inventor of the "tuned track," a special springy running surface installed in Harvard's Gordon indoor track and tennis facility. Subsequent tuned tracks were installed at Yale University and at Madison Square Garden in New York and are credited with improving running times as well as cutting in half the number of injuries.<ref name="Thomas">{{cite news |last1=Thomas |first1=Robert McG. Jr. |title=Thomas McMahon, 55, Scientist-Author, Dies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/02/19/us/thomas-mcmahon-55-scientist-author-dies.html |access-date=21 February 2023 |work=The New York Times |date=19 February 1999}}</ref>

McMahon wrote four well-regarded novels, the last published posthumously.  ''Loving Little Egypt'' won the 1988 Rosenthal Award from the [[American Academy of Arts and Letters]].<ref name="Howe"/><ref name="Kunkel"/> Characters in McMahon's novels are also credited with inventions, for example the [[odor amplifier]].

==Novels==
* ''Principles of American Nuclear Chemistry: A Novel'' (1970), [[Little, Brown and Company]], {{ISBN|0-226-56110-0}}.<ref name="Thomas"/>
* ''McKay's Bees'' (1979), [[Harper & Row]], {{ISBN|0-226-56111-9}}.<ref name="Thomas"/>
* ''Loving Little Egypt'' (1987), [[Viking Press]], {{ISBN|0-226-56109-7}}.<ref name="Thomas"/>
* ''Ira Foxglove'' (2004), Brook Street Press, {{ISBN|0-9724295-3-0}}.<ref name="Kunkel">{{cite web |last1=Kunkel |first1=Karl |title=Review of Ira Foxglove |url=https://www.forewordreviews.com/reviews/ira-foxglove/ |website=Foreword Reviews|date=2004 |access-date=21 February 2023 |language=en}}</ref>
